extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers writing academic research reports and papers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, drafting, and revising introductions, conclusions, titles, and sentences in academic research reports, with principles for clarity, pacing, and style. Emphasizes diagnosing and revising unclear sentences and structuring openings and closings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full introduction: Context + Problem + Response
rubrics_metrics.description: A full introduction consists of just three elements: Context + Problem + Response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't need all three in every report: omit the common ground if the problem is well known; omit consequences if they are well known; if you want readers to follow your thinking before they know your answer, offer a launching point at the end of your introduction and state your main point in your conclusion. The pattern is formulaic but useful as a thinking tool to identify what readers know and should know.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid point-last launching that only promises a point
rubrics_metrics.description: An introduction that merely promises a point to come (a 'point-last paper') is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must save your point for the end, the launching point must do more than announce a general topic — it should suggest conceptual outlines of your solution or announce a plan. Example anti-pattern: 'This study investigates processes leading to ozone depletion.' Better: preview conceptual approach or specific plan (e.g., list models to be evaluated and criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer a launching plan when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If you announce a plan in the introduction, show what you will do (e.g., evaluate three computer models to determine cost-effectiveness in reliability, speed, and ease of use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'plan' opening is common in social sciences but can seem ham-handed in the humanities. Use it when it helps readers anticipate structure and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set the pace of your introduction to audience knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: How quickly to raise your problem depends on how much your readers know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open quickly when addressing knowledgeable peers (implies familiarity); open slowly (providing background/definitions) when readers know less. Opening too slowly for knowledgeable readers implies you know little; opening too quickly for novices seems inconsiderate. It's a 'Goldilocks' decision: match pace to audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit elements when they are already known
rubrics_metrics.description: If the problem is well known, omit the common ground; if the consequences are well known, omit them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the introduction length and content to what your expected readers already know to avoid redundancy and to maintain appropriate pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start conclusion with your main point
rubrics_metrics.description: State your main point near the beginning of your conclusion. If you already stated it in the introduction, repeat it here but more fully; do not simply repeat it word-for-word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conclusion serves to present the point more fully and should not be a verbatim repetition of the introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add a new significance or application in the conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: After your point, say why it's significant, preferably with a new answer to 'So what?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce an additional implication or consequence (e.g., legislative or cultural effects) but take care not to broaden that significance so much that it appears to be your main point — introduce it 'almost by the way' as an additional implication. You may choose to save volatile implications for the conclusion rather than the introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude by calling for more research
rubrics_metrics.description: Your conclusion can call for research still to do, stating what remains to be studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest specific follow-ups (e.g., longitudinal studies on mentoring) to keep the conversation alive and guide interested readers on next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichéd or inappropriate openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't start with a dictionary entry, grandiose 'The most profound...' openings, or simply repeat the assignment language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you're stuck, paraphrase the assignment to prime writing but rewrite it in revision. Clichés and grand openings weaken credibility; choose openings that anticipate key terms and fit the topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good opening choices: fact, quotation, or anecdote (with conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three standard choices for first sentences: open with a striking fact relevant to your problem; open with a striking quotation; open with a relevant anecdote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a quotation only if its words anticipate key terms in the rest of your introduction. Use an anecdote only if its language anticipates your topic and vividly illustrates your problem. Examples provided illustrate when each is effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Echo opening in the final words
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring a report to a close by echoing your opening fact, anecdote, or quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An echoing device ties opening and conclusion together and can be literary without being inappropriate for academic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the title last and make it informative
rubrics_metrics.description: The title is the first thing readers read and the last you should write; a title should help readers understand specifically what is to come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put key words from your main point in the title. Two-line titles give room for key terms; end the first line with a colon to introduce a more specific second line. Avoid vague single-word titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear, concise, direct sentence style
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers prefer sentences that sound like one colleague speaking to another (clear and direct) over ones that sound like a machine or an overly simplified teacher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly convoluted 'academic' prose that masks sloppy thinking. Complex thought sometimes requires complex style, but most dense academic writing reflects poor revision. Aim for clarity without oversimplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 1: Make subjects name main characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers will judge sentences to be clear and readable to the degree that you make their subjects name the main characters in your story. Subjects should be short, specific, and concrete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects that name concrete characters (people, institutions, things) make the story easier to follow than abstract nominal subjects (e.g., 'the reason for Locke's frequent repetition').

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 2: Express crucial actions as verbs (avoid nominalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Express crucial actions in verbs rather than as abstract nouns; nominalizations (decision → decision) make sentences cluttered and vague.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nominalizations add articles and prepositions and often force vague verbs like 'made' to do the work of several specific verbs. Typical nominalization suffixes: -tion, -ness, -ment, -ence, -ity. Two practical rules: express actions with verbs and make central characters the subjects of those verbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose unclear sentences with the 'first six or seven words' test
rubrics_metrics.description: To diagnose: underline the first six or seven words of every clause and test (a) are the underlined subjects concrete characters? and (b) do the underlined verbs name specific actions rather than general ones ('have', 'make', 'do', 'be')?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a sentence fails either test, revise. Revision steps: find the characters you want to tell a story about (or invent them), find what those characters are doing (change noun-actions into verbs), and create clauses with main characters as subjects and their actions as verbs. You will often recast sentences into If X, then Y; X because Y; Although X, Y formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who/what can be a character: concrete or abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'character' can be people, things, or even abstractions if you can make them the subject of many verbs; experts often tell stories about abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All things being equal, readers prefer flesh-and-blood characters. But in specialist contexts, abstract characters (e.g., standardized indices) may be appropriate and need not be revised. Use judgement about when abstractions are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive abstraction in subject position
rubrics_metrics.description: The worst problem is making abstract nouns your main characters and surrounding them with other abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your best central character is an abstraction, avoid adding more unnecessary abstract nouns. Know which abstractions to keep and which to change into verbs — this skill develops with practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create main characters deliberately by subject choice
rubrics_metrics.description: You can make any character the main character of a sentence by choosing it as the subject; pick the subject to guide readers' perception of whom or what the story is about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'If developers strip rain forests...' vs 'If Brazil strips its rain forests...' — choose the subject (developers, loggers, Brazil) to emphasize whom you want readers to consider responsible or central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 3: Old-before-new (begin sentences with familiar information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers follow a story most easily if each sentence begins with information familiar to them (usually something mentioned before); put unpredictable or complex information at the end of the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnosis: underline first six or seven words and check whether they are familiar. Revision: make sentence openings refer to familiar information (often your main characters repeated or recalled from previous sentences) and place new/unexpected information at sentence ends. This principle interacts with subject-as-character guidance; if in conflict, prefer old-before-new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active vs. passive to place familiar information appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't follow a blanket rule to avoid passive voice — instead ask whether sentences begin with familiar information or a main character. Use passive when it lets you begin with older, more familiar information; use active when the action is tied to the author/researcher (rhetorical actions) or when specific agency matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive is useful to move older information to the sentence beginning and improve flow. Use active first-person ('we') appropriately for actions only the authors can perform (e.g., conclude, design experiments); the passive can signal repeatability of processes (e.g., 'Eye movements were measured...'). Avoid dogmatic prescriptions about voice; choose to serve clarity and rhetorical appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision priority: revise sentences, not during drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't try to apply these sentence-revision principles as you draft new sentences; use them when revising after you have sentences to revise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying these rules in drafting may tie you in knots. Reserve them for revision passes to improve clarity and flow.
